title: Soft Geometric Inductive Bias for Object Centric Dynamics
claim: A soft-structured model beats both unstructured and strictly constrained baselines across diverse domains, with lower error and variance.
layout: 3 horizontal box-plot panels, left-to-right, shared method rows, orange highlights ours
description: Three side-by-side horizontal box-plot panels titled Rigid body (2D), Charged n-body (3D), and WOMD. Each panel compares three models on the y-axis: S-Clifford-Transformer (orange), E-Clifford-Transformer (blue), and Transformer (green). The x-axes show rollout RMSE for the first two panels and ADE in meters for the third, with light vertical gridlines. In every panel the orange S-Clifford box sits farthest left, at the lowest error, and it is narrow. The blue and green boxes sit at higher error, and their order differs by panel. Some boxes have wide whiskers, such as the green Transformer in the rigid-body panel and the blue E-Clifford in the n-body and WOMD panels. The eye goes to the orange box at the left of each panel. The plots have a clean white background and no other decoration.
caption: Rollout RMSE and average displacement error (ADE) for autoregressive object-centric world models trained on 2D rigid body physics with collisions (left), 3D charged particles in harmonic potential (middle), and real-world multi-agent driving scenarios from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD) (right). Our Clifford transformer with a soft geometric inductive bias (S-CliffordTransformer) outperforms the vanilla transformer (Transformer) and the equivariant Clifford transformer (E-CliffordTransformer) in all data domains.
abstract: Physical systems are naturally parameterized in terms of geometric entities and their transformations. While exact equivariance can be a powerful inductive bias, real-world applications frequently exhibit approximate or broken symmetries in practice. We introduce object-centric world models that provide a soft geometric inductive bias without enforcing exact symmetries. By embedding object states as Clifford multivectors, our models encourage physically meaningful transformations while retaining the expressivity needed to handle asymmetric dynamics. We evaluate our approach on 2D rigid-body dynamics, 3D charged-particle systems, and real-world driving trajectories. Compared to both unstructured baselines and strictly equivariant models, our soft Clifford transformer achieves better long-horizon fidelity, particularly in regimes with broken symmetries. These results suggest that geometric algebra offers an effective middle ground, delivering sample-efficient dynamics without the inflexibility of hard mathematical constraints.
